title: 14  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
section: 14.2 A report is an argument supported by evidence
text:
14.2 A report is an argument supported by evidence
A useful report states a question, describes data and design, explains decisions, presents results, and discusses limitations. Embedding R code keeps numerical evidence connected to its computation. If a dataset changes, re-rendering updates the results. This reduces transcription errors but cannot correct an unsuitable analysis.
R Markdown usually uses .Rmd source files and rmarkdown::render(). Quarto uses .qmd source files and the quarto render command. Both can execute R through knitr. Their configuration differs: R Markdown uses output: whereas Quarto uses format:. Simply renaming an old bookdown file is not a complete migration; chapter configuration, references, chunk options, and dependencies need checking.
crumbs: 14  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto

title: 14  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
14.3 Anatomy of a Quarto document
The following is a complete small document. The YAML header defines metadata and formats, ordinary Markdown supplies prose, and the R chunk computes a table. Save it as report.qmd in the project folder. The separate practicals/report.qmd provides a fuller working example.
---
title: "Plant growth: a reproducible analysis"
author: "Student name"
format:
  html: default
  pdf: default
  docx: default
---

# Question

How do dry-weight measurements vary among the documented groups?

::: {#tbl-weight .cell tbl-cap='Mean dry weight by group in PlantGrowth.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
data("PlantGrowth", package = "datasets")
tab <- aggregate(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth, mean)
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|group | weight|
|:-----|------:|
|ctrl  |   5.03|
|trt1  |   4.66|
|trt2  |   5.53|


:::
:::

Interpret the estimates in @tbl-weight using the dataset documentation.
Use descriptive chunk labels; figure labels begin with fig- and table labels with tbl- for cross-references. A figure chunk can use #| fig-cap: "...". A hidden setup chunk may set #| include: false, but keep the source available to readers. echo: false hides code, not results. eval: false displays an example without executing it. Avoid hiding warnings until they have been investigated.

14.6 Render and share
Run shell commands in the Terminal, not in the R Console:
quarto preview
quarto render --to html
quarto render --to docx
quarto render --to pdf
quarto render practicals/report.qmd --to html
PDF output requires a working LaTeX distribution, for example TinyTeX installed through quarto install tinytex. Install it only if PDF is needed. HTML is the default classroom format in the README instructions. Rendering the entire book to Word or PDF combines chapters into a single document. Opening an HTML file locally is not the same as publishing it to a public server.
Before sharing, restart R and render from source. Include source files, permitted data, metadata, package requirements, and instructions. sessionInfo() records R and loaded package versions. title: 14  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
14.7 Building the report in stages
Let us develop a report in the same order as an analysis. First create the document with its question, data source, and design, even before the final model is chosen. Then add a data-check section, followed by descriptive tables and figures. Only after examining those results should the methods and model sections be completed. This sequence makes the scientific argument visible rather than hiding it behind a final table of p-values.
An effective data section identifies the observational unit, sample size, variable units, collection period, and treatment or sampling scheme. State how the raw file was obtained and whether permission is needed to share it. In the cleaning section, explain missingness, corrections, and exclusions with their consequences for the analysis. Avoid including personal or confidential identifiers merely because they happen to be in the original spreadsheet.
The methods section should name the response, predictors or factors, model, and assumptions in terms that match the actual code. If the text describes a paired test but the code fits an unpaired test, a successful render has reproduced an inconsistency. Read both parts together. The results section should lead with the size and direction of important effects, followed by uncertainty and evidence. Keep mechanistic explanations and generalization limits in the discussion.

title: 14  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
14.8 Managing code chunks and dependencies
Each document is easiest to understand when it can be executed from top to bottom in a new session. The first chunk loads packages and reads inputs. Later chunks depend on those named objects. Avoid loading data by hand into the Environment pane and then assuming they will be available during rendering.


::: {#tbl-treatment-means .cell tbl-cap='Mean simulated grain yield by management treatment.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
means <- trial |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_yield = mean(yield_t_ha), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(means, digits = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|treatment |  n| mean_yield|
|:---------|--:|----------:|
|Compost   | 20|       3.84|
|Control   | 20|       3.12|
|Mineral   | 20|       4.36|


:::
:::
The setup chunk is hidden in the displayed report but remains in the source. It does not install packages. The table chunk visibly records the summary operation. A future reader can distinguish a count of plot records from an estimate of mean yield and can rerun both.
Caching and freezing can save time in large projects, but they can also leave stale output when dependencies are misunderstood. During textbook revision, this project uses freeze: false so examples are executed again. Do not use old cached results to claim that revised code has been checked. For serious projects, record the environment and consider a lockfile, while recognizing that external data sources can change independently of package versions.

title: 14  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
14.9 Tables, figures, and numerical precision
A table title should say what was measured, how observations were grouped, and what the numbers represent. Put units in column headings where possible. Report enough digits for interpretation without suggesting unrealistic measurement precision. A yield measured to 0.01 t/ha should not normally be presented to eight decimal places merely because R printed them.
A figure caption should allow the graph to be understood away from the surrounding paragraph. Distinguish observed points from fitted lines, and describe error bars or shaded intervals precisely. “Error bars” is insufficient: are they SD, SE, confidence intervals, or prediction intervals? If an interactive figure permits hovering, retain axis labels and a caption so the static version remains meaningful.
Cross-references are preferable to manually typed numbers. After inserting a new table, @tbl-treatment-means updates its reference automatically. Manually writing “Table 3” can become wrong after reorganization. The same applies to chapter references and figure references. The final review should include checking that a referenced object actually supports the claim made in the sentence.

title: 14  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
section: 14.10 Reproducibility is also a classroom assessment
text:
14.10 Reproducibility is also a classroom assessment
Ask a classmate to open a copy of the complete project, restart R, and render the report. If it fails, identify whether the missing component is a file, package, path, or undocumented manual step. Record the correction in the project instead of asking the classmate to imitate your Console history.
Finally, read the rendered document as a reader. Are headings in a logical order? Do tables fit? Are captions readable? Do the conclusions match the estimates? A report can be computationally reproducible and scientifically weak, or scientifically thoughtful but computationally incomplete. Undergraduate training should develop both skills together.

B.3 Graphics, description, and EDA

soil <- read.csv("data/soil.csv")
x <- soil$available_n_mg_kg
c(mean = mean(x), median = median(x), variance = var(x), sd = sd(x), IQR = IQR(x))

37.56500 37.05000 58.55723  7.65227 10.62500 

table(soil$soil_class)


 Clay loam       Loam Sandy loam 
        20         20         20 


Nitrogen means, medians, SDs, and IQRs have units mg/kg; variance has units (mg/kg)². An extreme positive value generally shifts the mean and SD more than the median and IQR. More observations can improve precision of a mean without reducing biological variability among individual observations. Leaves from the same treated plant are subsamples unless treatment was independently assigned at the leaf level and the analysis supports that design.
An EDA memo should identify treatment–nitrogen confounding, variation among blocks, the simulated source, and the observational unit. Numerical summaries must be taken from executed output. A pooled nitrogen–yield trend cannot separate management components that vary together.

title: Appendix B — Selected exercise solutions
text:
B.4 Growth and time series

growth <- read.csv("data/growth.csv")
fit <- nls(biomass_g_m2 ~ A / (1 + exp(-k * (day - ti))), growth,
           start = list(A = 1000, k = .07, ti = 50))
predict(fit, data.frame(day = 75))

[1] 861.3136


Day 75 is inside the observed 10–120 day range, so this is interpolation. It estimates a mean curve response under the model, not an exact new quadrat measurement. The logistic inflection biomass is A/2; the Gompertz value is A/e. A fit based only on early observations may not identify the plateau reliably.
For forecasting, use the first eight years as training and the last two as holdout, as in Chapter 10. Report test MAE/RMSE for both methods. Fitting on all ten years first would let future information affect model selection and estimates. A centred moving average includes future values and is not a directly available real-time predictor.

B.5 Inference, ANOVA, and regression

data("PlantGrowth", package = "datasets")
fit_aov <- aov(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth)
df.residual(fit_aov)

[1] 27

TukeyHSD(fit_aov)

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)

$group
            diff        lwr       upr     p adj
trt1-ctrl -0.371 -1.0622161 0.3202161 0.3908711
trt2-ctrl  0.494 -0.1972161 1.1852161 0.1979960
trt2-trt1  0.865  0.1737839 1.5562161 0.0120064


The one-way global null is equality of the three population group means. There are 27 residual degrees of freedom. A Tukey interval excluding zero indicates evidence of a difference for that pair under the simultaneous procedure and its assumptions. A p-value of 0.08 is not proof of no effect; the effect estimate and interval show which magnitudes remain compatible with the data.
The paired soil test matches the same plots before and after. An unpaired analysis discards that pairing. The pest table has independent plot statuses as its units; expected counts must be inspected before trusting a chi-square approximation.
In regression, a rainfall coefficient is a conditional change in predicted mean yield per millimetre, holding nitrogen fixed. A prediction interval is wider than a confidence interval because it also represents individual-outcome variation. A random row split is inappropriate when observations from the same farm, future period, or nearby spatial cluster would leak information across training and test sets.

title: Appendix C — Glossary and R reference
text:
Term
Meaning in this book




Population
The set of units about which a question is asked; define its crop, place, time, and management scope.


Sample
Observed units selected from a population. Convenience samples can limit generalization.


Experimental unit
Smallest unit independently assigned a treatment.


Observational unit
Unit on which a measurement is recorded; it may be a subsample of an experimental unit.


Replication
Independent repetition of treatment assignment at the experimental-unit level.


Randomization
A chance-based assignment procedure that helps separate treatment from nuisance influences.


Blocking
Grouping comparable experimental units before randomization to account for known variation.


Confounding
A situation where influences vary together so their separate contributions cannot be identified from the comparison.


Parameter
A quantity describing a population or a model, such as a mean or regression slope.


Estimate
A value calculated from data to represent a parameter.


Residual
Observed response minus its fitted model value.


Standard deviation
Spread among observations, in the measurement’s units.


Standard error
Estimated sampling variation of a statistic, such as an estimated mean.


Confidence interval
An interval constructed by a procedure with stated repeated-sampling coverage under assumptions.


Prediction interval
An interval for a new response, including individual-response variation under a model.


Effect size
Magnitude of a difference or association; its practical relevance depends on context and units.


p-value
Tail probability for a statistic under a specified null model and assumptions.


Interpolation
Prediction within the observed predictor domain.


Extrapolation
Prediction beyond the observed domain; it requires additional justification.


Holdout
Observations reserved from fitting for assessing prediction.


Reproducibility
Ability to regenerate an analysis from its inputs, code, and environment.

C.3 Common errors and a repair sequence
When a command fails, read the first error, check spelling and object existence, inspect types and dimensions, and run the smallest relevant part. For file errors, check getwd() and file.exists(). For a missing package, check installation and loading. For a model failure, inspect the data and the model assumptions before changing optimizer settings. Keep a short note of the cause and resolution; debugging is a skill developed through explanation.

C.4 Before you submit an analysis
State the question and unit; document the source and units; retain raw data; record cleaning decisions; show distributions; justify the model; examine residuals; report effects and uncertainty; distinguish association from causation; and render from a fresh session. These steps are scientific habits, not a substitute for judgment.

title: 14  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
section: 14.13 Vibe coding and AI-assisted R programming
text:
14.13 Vibe coding and AI-assisted R programming

14.13.1 From an idea to a first draft
Vibe coding is an informal term for developing software by describing what you want in ordinary language, asking an AI system to generate code, running it, and requesting changes. The term is often associated with accepting implementation details without examining them closely. For a statistical analysis, we need to go further: understand the code, verify the calculations, and justify the model. In this book, we use the conversational approach as an entry into reviewed AI-assisted programming. See the overview of the term.
For example, a student might begin with “Make a colourful graph of crop yields.” An AI assistant can draft a plot quickly, but that request omits the data structure, units, experimental unit, and purpose. A graph of treatment means, a distribution of individual plot yields, and a fitted response curve answer different questions. Clear agricultural reasoning makes a better prompt and a better analysis.


14.13.2 Using AI with R
One approach is to ask an AI chat assistant for a small R code draft, inspect it, and run it in RStudio. Another is to use an assistant integrated into an R development environment. Current examples include Posit Assistant in RStudio and Positron; their capabilities, access requirements, and settings are described in the RStudio guide and Positron documentation. This lesson does not require a paid assistant or a particular model.
Begin with a small task: explain a function, summarize a table, improve axis labels, or diagnose a reproducible error. Ask for the reason behind each change. Read unfamiliar functions in R’s help system and confirm that suggested packages and arguments exist. A plausible function name is not evidence that a function is available.


14.13.3 Write a prompt that specifies the analysis






A model prompt for an agricultural practical



I am learning R. I have independent plot observations from a teaching experiment. The columns are treatment and yield_t_ha; yield is measured in tonnes per hectare. Use base R. Produce a table with total records, nonmissing yields, missing yields, mean, and standard deviation for each treatment. Keep missing values in the data and exclude them only from calculations that require observed yields. Do not replace missing values with zero, delete outliers, or run significance tests. Include a small simulated example, explain the code, and show how I can check the results manually.


Specify the question, experimental unit, column names and units, design, missing-value rule, and requested output. State restrictions such as “use base R” or “do not install packages.” Ask for one step at a time so you can inspect its result before proceeding. Share a small simulated example or a permitted, de-identified excerpt when explaining a problem; check your institution’s rules before sending research data to an external service.


14.13.4 Worked example: review a generated summary
The following is a teaching reference solution to the prompt, not a transcript of a particular AI response. The simulated data contain a missing yield in the Control group. We deliberately count both rows and observed yields so the denominator is visible.

ai_trial <- data.frame(
  treatment = c("Control", "Control", "Control", "Compost", "Compost", "Compost"),
  yield_t_ha = c(3.0, 4.0, NA, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0)
)

summarize_yield <- function(x) {
  observed <- x[!is.na(x)]
  c(total = length(x), observed = length(observed),
    missing = sum(is.na(x)),
    mean = if (length(observed)) mean(observed) else NA_real_,
    SD = if (length(observed) > 1) sd(observed) else NA_real_)
}

ai_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(ai_trial$yield_t_ha, ai_trial$treatment), summarize_yield
))
ai_summary

        total observed missing mean        SD
Compost     3        3       0  4.5 0.5000000
Control     3        2       1  3.5 0.7071068

# Independent checks against calculations we can do by hand
stopifnot(ai_summary["Control", "total"] == 3,
          ai_summary["Control", "observed"] == 2,
          ai_summary["Control", "missing"] == 1,
          isTRUE(all.equal(unname(ai_summary["Control", "mean"]), 3.5)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(unname(ai_summary["Compost", "mean"]), 4.5)))

The Control mean is \((3+4)/2=3.5\) t/ha. Dividing by three, or replacing the missing observation with zero, would answer a different question. Its sample SD is approximately 0.707 t/ha; the Compost SD is 0.5 t/ha. With no observed yields, the mean is undefined; with only one observed yield, the sample SD is undefined. The function returns NA for those cases. Summary values alone do not demonstrate a treatment effect.


14.13.5 Refine, debug, and verify
Useful follow-up prompts include:

“Explain why the number of observed yields differs from the number of records.”
“My error is object 'yield' not found. Here is names(ai_trial) and the failing line. Explain the mismatch and change only that line.”
“Review this model for a randomized block experiment. Explain how the block factor enters the formula before changing the code.”
“Add units and a caption to this plot without changing the observations or fitted model.”

When a draft fails, provide the exact error and the smallest example that reproduces it. Avoid repeatedly asking an assistant to repair a long script without checking what it changes. A coding error and a statistical error are different: aov(yield ~ treatment) can execute successfully while omitting a block factor required by the design. A paired test, an independent-samples test, and a repeated-measures model are not interchangeable repairs.






Successful execution is only the first check



Inspect row counts, units, missingness, group sizes, model formulas, and assumptions. Verify at least one result independently. Check that plots and written conclusions match the computed output. Do not ask AI to keep changing an analysis until a p-value becomes significant. You remain responsible for the method and interpretation.




14.13.6 Save a reproducible record
Keep the accepted R code in the project and render the report in a fresh session. Record package versions, relevant prompts, substantive AI contributions, and the corrections you made. Follow course and publication rules for acknowledging assistance. AI may help draft a methods paragraph, but the paragraph must describe the analysis actually performed. Never invent citations, observations, or results to complete a report.
Closing practical. Give an assistant the model prompt above, or write your own proposed solution if no assistant is available. Compare its code with the reference calculation. Test an all-missing group and a group with one observed yield. Submit the prompt, reviewed code, verification results, and a short account of what you accepted or corrected. Explain every line you submit.
